nodes.label: Tosti et al. (1991) reported a 4.5-year-old girl with Noonan syndrome and loose anagen hair. Her hair was short and blond, had never been cut, and was easily plucked. Trichogram showed that nearly all bulbs were abnormally shaped anagen bulbs lacking inner and outer root sheaths. Scalp biopsy showed marked cleft formation between fragmented inner root sheaths and irregularly shaped hair shafts.

Tosti et al. (1997) reported 19 patients diagnosed with loose anagen hair (LAH) at a university medical center beginning in 1990: 14 children and 5 adults, aged 8 months to 47 years. Associated diseases included Noonan syndrome in a 5-year-old boy and alopecia areata in a 3-year-old boy. In all cases a trichogram showed mostly anagen hairs (80 to 100%) without sheaths.

Among the patients with LAH reported by Tosti et al. (1997), 2 adults were parents of 2 affected children. The other 3 adults were the only members of their families with LAH. The authors concluded that LAH may be sporadic, may occur together with developmental or acquired conditions, or, less commonly, may be familial.

Tosti et al. (1997) found that LAH can begin in adulthood: 3 sporadic adults had diffuse hair shedding that started suddenly 1 to 3 years before evaluation. They noted that adult-onset LAH can easily be misdiagnosed as telogen hair loss. On follow-up, LAH stayed stable in 4 children and 1 adult, and hair density improved considerably in 2 children and 1 adult.

Tosti et al. (1997) studied the pathology of hair from 5 patients. Apart from frequent fragmentation of the inner root sheath, they found no morphologic abnormalities of the hair follicles. They concluded that pathologic findings are of little diagnostic value in LAH.

Mazzanti et al. (2003) described 3 children with short stature, the same facial phenotype, macrocephaly, enlarged cerebrospinal fluid spaces, short neck with redundant skin, severe growth hormone deficiency, and mild psychomotor delay with attention deficit-hyperactivity disorder (ADHD). Two of the children had mild dilatation of the pulmonary root. All 3 had a unique combination of ectodermal abnormalities, including darkly pigmented hairless skin and hair defined as loose anagen hair.

Mazzanti et al. (2003) concluded that the children's appearance, which was not completely typical of Noonan syndrome, together with the behavioral phenotype, GH deficiency, darkly pigmented hairless skin, and loose anagen hair, did not fit any known condition. They postulated that the children might represent a distinct, previously unreported syndrome, which they proposed to name 'Noonan-like syndrome with loose anagen hair.'

Cordeddu et al. (2009) used an in silico protein network analysis seeded with known RAS/MAPK mutant proteins to prioritize SHOC2 as a candidate Noonan syndrome gene. Sequencing of SHOC2 in 96 Noonan syndrome patients negative for mutations in known genes identified a heterozygous 4A-G transition predicting a ser2-to-gly (S2G) substitution in 4 unrelated sporadic individuals; the mutation was absent from the parents in the 3 families tested (paternity confirmed), indicating de novo origin, and was present in several tissues, indicating germline transmission.

Cordeddu et al. (2009) analyzed SHOC2 in a further 410 mutation-negative subjects with Noonan syndrome or a related phenotype and found the 4A>G (S2G) change in 21, with de novo occurrence proven in the 12 families with available parental DNA. No other disease-associated SHOC2 variant was found, suggesting a specific pathogenetic role for S2G; in total 25 subjects shared the mutation.

Cordeddu et al. (2009) found that SHOC2 S2G mutation-positive individuals shared a consistent phenotype previously termed Noonan-like syndrome with loose anagen hair: Noonan-like facies (macrocephaly, high forehead, hypertelorism, ptosis, low-set posteriorly rotated ears, short webbed neck, pectus anomalies), reduced growth frequently with proven GH deficiency, cognitive deficits, hyperactive behavior that improved with age, and easily pluckable, sparse, thin, slow-growing hair, with loose anagen hair confirmed microscopically in 12. Most had darkly pigmented skin with eczema or ichthyosis, cardiac anomalies were common with mitral valve dysplasia and septal defects overrepresented, and the voice was hypernasal. Several were thought to resemble Costello or cardiofaciocutaneous syndrome in infancy.

Cordeddu et al. (2009) showed that the S2G substitution creates an N-myristoylation site: SHOC2 S2G expressed in Cos-1 cells incorporated [3H]-myristic acid, whereas wildtype SHOC2 and a disease-unrelated S2A mutant did not.

Cordeddu et al. (2009) found that wildtype SHOC2 was distributed in cytoplasm and nucleus in starved Cos-1 cells and translocated to the nucleus upon EGF stimulation (also seen for endogenous SHOC2 in primary fibroblasts), whereas SHOC2 S2G was constitutively targeted to the plasma membrane, dependent on myristoylation (reversed by an NMT inhibitor), and failed to translocate to the nucleus. The mutant did not heterodimerize with wildtype, excluding a dominant-negative effect, and it enhanced EGF-dependent ERK phosphorylation in Neuro2A cells but not in Cos-1 or 293T cells, indicating cell type-specific MAPK activation.

Cordeddu et al. (2009) found in C. elegans that wildtype human SHOC2, but not S2G, could functionally replace SUR-8 in a sur-8rf;let-60gof background, and S2G did not act as a dominant negative. Expression of SHOC2 S2G or myristoylation-tagged wildtype SHOC2 at early L3 caused protruding vulva, egg-laying defects and bag-of-worms phenotypes due to abnormal vulval morphogenesis (asymmetric invaginations involving P5.p/P7.p descendants in 17/48 S2G larvae), without altered vulval cell fate specification; these proteins were membrane-targeted in worm cells.

Komatsuzaki et al. (2010) analyzed SHOC2 in 92 patients with Noonan syndrome and related disorders who did not have mutations in PTPN11, KRAS, HRAS, BRAF, MAP2K1/2, SOS1, or RAF1, and found the previously identified p.S2G mutation in 8 patients.

Komatsuzaki et al. (2010) reported that all 8 patients with the SHOC2 p.S2G mutation had short stature, sparse hair, and atopic skin; 6 had severe mental retardation and easily pluckable hair, and 1 had leukocytosis. The authors concluded that easily pluckable/loose anagen hair is distinctive in SHOC2 mutation-positive patients, whose features partially overlap with typical Noonan or CFC syndrome.
Komatsuzaki et al. (2010) developed a rapid melting curve analysis-based detection system for the SHOC2 p.S2G mutation for screening of this apparently common mutation.
Komatsuzaki et al. (2010) identified no SHOC2 mutations in leukemia cells from 82 leukemia patients.

Hoban et al. (2012) reported a male infant with Noonan syndrome due to a SHOC2 mutation. He was delivered prematurely at 32 weeks because of fetal distress. After birth he had dysmorphic features, edema, hepatosplenomegaly, leukocytosis, thrombocytopenia, and respiratory distress. An echocardiogram showed hypertrophic cardiomyopathy with left ventricular outflow tract obstruction. The cardiac lesion progressed quickly, and he was discharged home for palliative care. The authors stated that his cardiac findings and features were not typical of individuals previously reported with this mutation and thus expanded the clinical phenotype.

In this infant with Noonan syndrome and fatal hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, Hoban et al. (2012) identified a de novo missense mutation in SHOC2 predicting p.Ser2Gly. It was found by clinical testing of genes that cause Noonan syndrome and related disorders. The authors noted that this pathogenic mutation had been reported before.

Gripp et al. (2013) reported 5 male patients with Noonan syndrome with loose anagen hair carrying the SHOC2 p.Ser2Gly mutation. All 5 had skin hyperpigmentation, sparse light-colored hair, increased fine wrinkles, ligamentous laxity and developmental delay. All 4 who were assessed had a structural cardiac anomaly. Hypotonia and macrocephaly were each present in 4 of 5. Polyhydramnios, increased birth weight and feeding tube use were each present in 3 of 5. All had unusually long eyelashes (dolichocilia).

Gripp et al. (2013) described distinctive brain abnormalities in patients with SHOC2 mutations. These were relative megalencephaly with enlarged subarachnoid spaces suggestive of benign external hydrocephalus, and a relatively small posterior fossa indicated by a vertical tentorium (4 of 4). The authors suggested that this combination accounted for the high rate of cerebellar tonsillar ectopia (3 of 4). Including literature cases, 3 of 8 patients who had MRI showed a Chiari I malformation.

Gripp et al. (2013) described patient 1, a boy born to 37-year-old parents after a pregnancy complicated by polyhydramnios and cystic hygroma. He was macrosomic at birth and had pyloric stenosis, severe failure to thrive needing a gastrostomy tube, mild pulmonic valve stenosis, low axial tone, small optic nerves, motor delay, and an OFC of +3 SD. At age 2 years 3 months, juvenile myelomonocytic leukemia was suspected. He developed hepatosplenomegaly, and bone marrow biopsy was most consistent with primary myelofibrosis, with a normal karyotype, no monosomy 7 and no JAK2 p.Val617Phe mutation. He died at age 2.5 years after splenectomy done in preparation for bone marrow transplant. This was the first hematologic neoplasm reported with a SHOC2 mutation.

In 5 patients with Noonan syndrome with loose anagen hair, Gripp et al. (2013) identified the recurrent SHOC2 c.4A>G mutation (p.Ser2Gly). In patient 1, it was found by postmortem testing of buccal DNA and was absent from both parents. The mutation was also de novo in patient 2. Sequencing of other RASopathy genes was normal in the patients.

Gripp et al. (2013) described patient 4, a boy of Mexican ancestry with global developmental delay and mild to moderate intellectual disability. He had an ASD, blond, sparse, easily pluckable hair, and long eyelashes. Brain MRI showed mild ventriculomegaly, periventricular nodular heterotopia, and a thick, dysplastic corpus callosum. By age 6 years he had developed a Chiari I malformation with platybasia and basilar invagination, along with C3–C4 vertebral fusion and unusual venous sinus anatomy. Periventricular nodular heterotopia had not previously been reported with a SHOC2 mutation.

Gripp et al. (2013) described patient 3, a boy with biventricular hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and right bundle branch block at age 6 months, later aortic insufficiency and mild pulmonic stenosis, and an OFC of +5 SD at age 9 years. He had severe aggressive behavior and was diagnosed with pervasive developmental disorder and Tourette syndrome, for which he took psychotropic medication.

Gripp et al. (2013) noted that patient 1 lacked the common somatic JAK2 mutation, which is present in most patients with myelofibrosis. They suggested that germline or somatic SHOC2 mutation, through activation of the RAS/MAPK pathway, may be causally involved in myelofibrosis.

Gripp et al. (2013) noted that 4 of their 5 patients had originally been suspected of having Costello syndrome. They subjectively observed that the ectodermal, growth and developmental features of SHOC2 p.Ser2Gly patients closely resembled those of Costello syndrome due to HRAS p.Gly13Cys, and they supported a gene panel approach to molecular testing.

Gripp et al. (2013) combined earlier case series (12 of 188 mutation-negative Noonan or Noonan-like patients) to estimate that SHOC2 mutations account for about 6% of mutation-negative Noonan syndrome. This corresponds to about 1.8% of all individuals with Noonan syndrome.

Hannig et al. (2014) reported a 5-year-old girl of European ancestry, born to nonconsanguineous parents, who had right optic nerve hypoplasia, bilateral nystagmus, speech delay, poor hair growth, and hyperactive behavior. She had average stature, macrocephaly (98th percentile), sparse and slow-growing hair that was not loose, normal skin pigmentation, bilateral ptosis, widely spaced nipples, and clubbed nails. MRI showed multiple irregularities of unknown significance in the midbrain, pons, and medulla. She did not have short stature, a cardiac anomaly, hyperpigmentation, ichthyosis, or loose anagen hair.

Hannig et al. (2014) found that the proband's father, who carried the same SHOC2 variant, was tall (6 feet 3 inches) and had intellectual disability, a high-arched palate, sparse hair, and clubbed nails. His features were very subtle and did not clearly indicate a RASopathy apart from the sparse hair and clubbed nails. Echocardiograms and renal ultrasounds were negative in both the father and the proband.

In the girl and her father, Hannig et al. (2014) found a heterozygous variant in the SHOC2 gene, c.519G>A (p.M173I), by sequencing a RASopathy gene panel. The proband inherited the variant from her father. It was not found in 6,500 asymptomatic individuals. Met173 is located in leucine-rich repeat 4 and is conserved among vertebrate SHOC2 orthologs.

Hannig et al. (2014) found that in SHOC2-depleted Cos1 cells, the M173I mutant restored EGF-induced ERK1/2 phosphorylation by only about 10% above basal levels, whereas wildtype SHOC2 fully rescued it. The mutant's half-life, subcellular localization, and binding to M-RAS and RAF1 were unchanged. However, it failed to precipitate PP1c effectively and produced only a mild increase in RAF1 Ser338 phosphorylation. The authors concluded that p.M173I causes loss of function in the ERK1/2 pathway.

Hannig et al. (2014) noted that patients with the M173I variant differed markedly from NS/LAH patients with the S2G mutation. The proband had NS-like craniofacial features and CFC-like sparse hair but did not have short stature, cardiac defects, or loose anagen hair. The authors concluded that SHOC2 mutations can cause a spectrum of RASopathy phenotypes of varying severity.

Bertola et al. (2017) reported a 12-year-old Brazilian boy with the recurrent p.Pro49Arg mutation in PPP1CB, a gene newly associated with RASopathies. He had sparse, thin, slow-growing hair resembling the ectodermal finding typical of Noonan syndrome-like disorder with loose anagen hair, and also had craniosynostosis. The authors concluded that PPP1CB-related Noonan syndrome with loose anagen hair shares great similarity with Noonan syndrome-like disorder with loose anagen hair.

Young et al. (2018) showed that MRAS interacts with SHOC2 and protein phosphatase 1 (PP1) to form a heterotrimeric holoenzyme that dephosphorylates the inhibitory S259 site on RAF kinases (S259 on CRAF, S365 on BRAF). MRAS and SHOC2 acted as PP1 regulatory subunits that make the complex highly specific for RAF. MRAS also acted as a targeting subunit, because the complex needed membrane localization to dephosphorylate RAF efficiently and to regulate the ERK pathway in cells.

Young et al. (2018) showed that Noonan syndrome mutations in SHOC2, MRAS and PPP1CB always promoted formation of the complex with the other two partners, but did not necessarily promote binding to other interactors. The authors concluded that Noonan syndrome in people with SHOC2, MRAS or PPP1CB mutations is likely driven at the biochemical level by enhanced ternary complex formation.

Young et al. (2018) reported that the predicted structure of SHOC2 closely resembles the A subunit of PP2A, which they suggested was a case of convergent structural evolution. They identified several regions in SHOC2 involved in complex formation, as well as residues in MRAS switch I and the interswitch region that help explain why MRAS binds specifically to SHOC2-PP1.
Motta et al. (2019) reported a third RASopathy-causing SHOC2 mutation, c.807_808delinsTT (p.Gln269_His270delinsHisTyr), which was associated with prenatal-onset hypertrophic cardiomyopathy.

Structural analyses by Motta et al. (2019) indicated that the SHOC2 Q269_H270delinsHY mutation might affect the relative orientation of the two leucine-rich repeat domains. Functional studies showed enhanced binding of the mutant protein to MRAS and PPP1CB and increased signaling through the MAPK cascade, supporting an activating role; unlike SHOC2 S2G, the mutant was not constitutively targeted to the plasma membrane.
Motta et al. (2019) concluded that diverse mechanisms of SHOC2 functional dysregulation converge toward upregulation of MAPK signaling.
